title: How Vampires Work
summary: Josh and Chuck return from a break (they recorded episodes in advance while filming their Science Channel TV show) and explore the history of vampires. They note common vampire traits (undead, blood-sucking, fear of crucifixes, garlic, holy water, night-only activity, invitation required to enter homes) and trace vampire-like folklore from ancient Mesopotamian demon Lamashtu and Jewish Lilith, through Greek Lamia, Indian rakshasa and vetala, Chinese kuei, to Eastern European upir and Romanian strigoi. They discuss how vampire beliefs arose to explain sudden death and disease, the 1850s New England vampire panic over tuberculosis, and the grave-desecration practices used against suspected vampires. They cover Bram Stoker's Dracula and its link to Vlad the Impaler, the shift to intelligent, reflection-less, charming vampires, and film adaptations (Nosferatu, Bela Lugosi's Dracula, Shadow of the Vampire, Lost Boys, Near Dark, True Blood, Twilight, Buffy). They also discuss psychic energy vampires and medical explanations such as porphyria, catalepsy, and decomposition. The episode closes with a horror fiction contest plug, and a listener mail trivia night segment from TomicCon in New York.
topics: Stuff You Should Know trivia night

segments.title: Return from break and TV show plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck explain that episodes were batch recorded while they filmed a Science Channel TV show, and briefly chat about Twilight and cable availability of the show.
topics: Stuff You Should Know TV show

segments.title: Vampire traits and ancient origins
segments.summary: The hosts list common vampire characteristics and note that vampire lore goes back as far as four thousand years, with the earliest vampires being demon goddesses such as Lamashtu from Mesopotamia who killed infants.

segments.title: Lilith and Lamia
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Lilith from Jewish texts, said to be Adam's first wife who left Eden and killed children, and Lamia, a Greek figure who killed children out of jealousy.

segments.title: Vampire-like creatures from India and China
segments.summary: The hosts describe the rakshasa and vetala from India and the Chinese kuei, corpses reanimated when the lower spirit failed to pass to the afterlife.

segments.title: Upir, kolyaks and Eastern European beliefs
segments.summary: Vampire beliefs spread to Europe via trade, centering on Central and Eastern Europe. The upir was a sinner, unbaptized baby, or non-Christian, and families dug up and staked suspected corpses; the upir was thought to return to the grave.

segments.title: New England vampire panic and disease explanations
segments.summary: Vampire panics often coincided with disease outbreaks. Examples include a sixteenth-century Venice corpse with a brick in its mouth and the 1850s Great New England Vampire Panic during a tuberculosis outbreak, when graves were dug up and hearts burned.

segments.title: Strigoi and Bram Stoker's Dracula
segments.summary: Romanian strigoi were described as going through stages and needing to be dealt with if they survived seven years. Bram Stoker researched Transylvania and based his Count Dracula partly on Vlad the Impaler, and Henry Irving was supposedly an inspiration.

segments.title: Vampire pop culture and films
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how Stoker introduced intelligent, charming, reflection-less vampires, and movies such as Bela Lugosi's Dracula, Nosferatu, Shadow of the Vampire, Lost Boys, Near Dark, True Blood, Twilight, and Buffy the Vampire Slayer.

segments.title: Psychic vampires and medical explanations
segments.summary: The hosts describe modern psychic energy vampires, then explain how porphyria, tuberculosis, catalepsy, and post-mortem changes like bloating and hair growth may have fed vampire beliefs.

segments.title: Horror fiction contest plug
segments.summary: Chuck plugs horror writer Christopher Kelly's novella Abraham Road and short story collection, both on Amazon.

segments.title: Listener mail: trivia night at TomicCon
segments.summary: Chuck reads listener emails from the TomicCon New York trivia night, including winning team Steve Holt and runners-up, and thanks the Cutting Room venue.
